overview.title: What is Glossa?
overview.p1: Glossa is an LLM-assisted translation workspace built for professional translators, philologists, and scholars working on long texts. The document is segmented into chunks, each chunk goes through a configurable pipeline, and the result is reviewed by an automatic judge.
overview.p2: The app is a local desktop application: projects, dictionaries, and prompt templates stay on your machine. Remote provider API keys are stored in the operating system keychain when available; if the keychain is inaccessible, Glossa uses an encrypted local file instead. Ollama lets you stay fully offline.
overview.step1: Import or paste the source document and tune segmentation in the import preview.
overview.step2: Pick Standard or Editorial mode and configure provider, model, and prompt for each stage.
overview.step3: Test the pipeline on a single chunk first (Test mode), then switch to Production mode to process the full document with real-time streaming.
overview.step4: The AI Judge evaluates each chunk; optionally, a coherence audit reviews the whole document.
overview.step5: Review and correct the candidate translation in the workspace, then re-evaluate or lock the chunk.
overview.step6: Export in .txt, .md, .html, .docx, or bilingual .md for publication or external review.
overview.p3: Provider and model are independent for every stage and for the judge: you can mix a fast model for translation with a stronger one for refine or audit, or stay fully local with Ollama.
overview.nav: Navigation: the breadcrumb at the top (Glossa // workspace // project) returns to home when you click the workspace. On the left there is a single bar: on the home it lists areas and workspaces (edit and delete of the active workspace live on its row); inside a project it holds Run, Pipeline, Document, Insight and Chunk. Run/Pipeline/Document open inside the bar; Insight, Chunk and the pipeline configuration open in a second panel alongside. Every bar resizes by dragging its right edge and collapses to icons; the edge is keyboard-reachable too (←/→ to resize, double-click to reset the width) and the project entries are navigable with the arrow keys. Loading a document keeps the view full: the Chunk panel opens only when you call it.

pipeline.title: Translation pipeline
pipeline.intro: The pipeline is the sequence of stages applied to each chunk. You configure it in the configuration panel (gear icon in the project sidebar), which has five tabs: Settings, Translation, Quality Control, Term Registry, and Prompt Preview.
pipeline.modesDesc: Pipeline mode is chosen in the Settings tab and defines which stages run on every chunk. The choice is locked once translations are in progress or complete.
pipeline.modeStandardDesc: A single translation pass followed by the judge. Fast and cheap, suited to drafts and technical text where a stylistic second pass isn't needed.
pipeline.modeEditorialDesc: Three-pass pipeline: an initial translation, a refine that improves rendering and fluency, and a format pass that only applies technical cleanup (punctuation, spacing, markdown) without seeing glossary or persona. Designed for literary or academic texts where quality matters more than cost.
pipeline.configDesc: In the Settings tab you pick source and target languages (swap button to reverse) and — optionally — a persona, a free-form system prompt opener describing voice, domain, and style of the translator. When the persona is active, the language pair is read from the persona itself.
pipeline.stagesDesc: In the Translation and Quality Control tabs you configure provider, model, prompt, and runtime parameters for each stage. Controls are identical across stages; what differs is the role (translation, refine, format, judge, coherence) and the default prompt seeded for it.
pipeline.previewDesc: The Prompt Preview tab shows the structure of the final prompt for every active stage: the cacheable part (system prompt + glossary + blob context), the stage instructions, the runtime blocks (source, previous stage result), and the glossary constraints. Use it to inspect exactly what will be sent to the model before launching the pipeline.
pipeline.runDesc: The run bar in the document workspace has a Test / Production toggle. In Test mode the pipeline runs on a single chunk and marks it as preview — configuration stays unlocked. When satisfied, switch to Production and click Play to process all ready chunks sequentially with token-level streaming; the judge runs automatically at the end. You can cancel at any time.
pipeline.editDesc: The candidate translation is editable inline. After manual corrections you can click 'Re-evaluate' in the audit panel to rerun the judge on the edited chunk only, or 'Lock translation' (green tick) to mark it final and protect it from accidental reprocessing.
pipeline.tipDesc: Use a fast model for translation (Gemini Flash, DeepSeek, light Ollama models), a capable model for refine (Claude Sonnet, GPT-5), a strict model for the judge. Stage choices are independent and costs are aggregated in the stats panel.

features.title: Features
features.intro: Reference of the most important areas of the interface. Each entry describes what it does, where it lives, and when it's useful.
features.documentWorkspaceDesc: The primary mode of the app. After importing a document, the workspace shows the current chunk with source and translation side by side, a top action bar to navigate and run the pipeline, and — on the right — the Insights panel with index, stats, audit, and logs. The mode is activated automatically when you load a document.
features.documentToolsDesc: Source and translation editors have a compact toolbar that can be collapsed when you want to read the clean text. On the candidate translation, the green tick locks it as final; each stage status badge opens a modal with the full output of that stage (trace), useful to see what the model actually produced.
features.markdownToolsDesc: The ? button in the editors opens this guide. The toolbar handles writing, preview, split view, text size, and essential Markdown formatting.
features.insightsDesc: Opens by clicking Insight in the project's left rail. Two levels: the Document panel (Index, Search, Stats, Coherence, Glossary) for whole-document metrics and search, and the Chunk panel (Summary, Audit, Notes, Operations) for the selected chunk. Selecting a chunk in the index automatically opens the Chunk level.
features.statsDesc: The Stats tab aggregates input and output tokens, estimated cost, and cache hit rate for the current session. The breakdown is per operation — each pipeline stage (e.g. Translation, Refine, Format), Audit, and Coherence — showing the model used and the percentage of tokens served from cache for each.
features.operationsLogDesc: The Operations tab in the Insights panel records every significant event: prompt sent, stage completion, errors, retries, audit, coherence. Each entry has a scope (pipeline / stage / audit / coherence), a level (info / success / warn / error), and — when relevant — the chunk involved. Prompt entries store the full system and user prompts in an expandable field, so you can inspect the exact request sent.
features.phraseMemoryDesc: Phrase Memory is specific to the translation workspace: it stores source phrase → translated phrase pairs and uses them to suggest consistent renderings in later documents in the same workspace. The Memory tab in the Insights panel shows matches for the current chunk and the button to explicitly save the current chunk to memory.
features.phraseMemoryAutomationDesc: When Phrase Memory is enabled, Glossa searches for matches in the background when the document opens or changes, but this search is read-only: it shows badges and suggestions, and does not modify translations or the database. Found matches are not added to the prompt until you select them; memory is written only through the 'Save chunk to memory' button. The translation lock remains an editorial marker only.
features.phraseMemoryTipDesc: If matches are visible but not selected, the pipeline runs without using them and Glossa warns you before launch. Use the checkboxes to decide what enters the prompt and save only translations you actually want to reuse.
features.configDrawerDesc: Opens with the gear icon. Five tabs: Settings (mode, language pair, persona, refine readiness), Translation (translation stage and refine/format when in editorial mode), Quality Control (judge and coherence prompts), Term Registry (glossary assigned to the project), Prompt Preview (preview of the final prompt for every stage).
features.modalsDesc: Settings, Library, Projects, Save dialog, Preflight check, and this guide share the same editorial shell: rounded border, header with icon and title, scrollable body, footer with a Close button and an X in the top-right. Every modal can be closed from either the X or the footer button.
features.appearanceDesc: Under Settings → Typography you choose the font for the whole interface among Plus Jakarta Sans (default), Geist, Inter, and IBM Plex Sans. The choice applies to the UI immediately and is remembered across sessions. Editorial serif values (italic headings and data) stay in Elstob and are left untouched. The same screen also holds the reading layout and highlight controls.
features.personaDesc: A persona is a free-form system prompt opener that replaces the default 'You are an expert X → Y translator'. You enable it in the Settings tab of the configuration panel. When active, the language pair is owned by the persona itself and per-stage overrides do not apply. Personas can be saved and loaded as templates.
features.templatesDesc: Every prompt — translation, audit, coherence, or persona — can be saved as a reusable template. The bookmark (+) saves the current prompt under a name; the open book loads a saved template. Templates are scoped by context (Stage / Audit / Persona): a template saved as Stage does not show up in the Audit picker and vice versa.
features.refineDesc: Next to every prompt sits a magic wand that sends the current text to an LLM to be rewritten. The provider and model used are shown as a `provider · model` label next to the button, so you always know what's doing the refining. The result replaces the prompt in the textarea — editable or undoable with Ctrl+Z.
features.refineGatingDesc: If the remote provider chosen for refinement has no API key configured, the wand button is disabled and the tooltip says so. Ollama is always enabled because it runs locally. In the Settings tab of the configuration panel, an inline notice lists the remote providers missing a key, or confirms that refinement is ready.
features.promptPreviewDesc: The Prompt Preview tab of the configuration panel shows, for each active stage, the structure of the prompt that will be sent: first the cacheable part (system prompt, glossary, blob context), then the stage-specific instructions, then the runtime blocks (source text, previous stage result, glossary constraints). Lets you see ordering, cacheable blocks, and placeholders without running the pipeline.
features.segmentationDesc: When you import a file (.txt, .md, .docx, .pdf), Glossa opens an import preview where you can fine-tune how the document is split into chunks before it enters the workspace. Segmentation in the workspace is fixed for that run: come back here if you want to change it.
features.segmentationControlsDesc: The icon bar provides: Auto-segment (scissors) — enables splitting by word count; Heading-aware (hash, Markdown only) — attaches standalone headings to the next paragraph so headings are never translated in isolation. The number field sets words per chunk (default in Settings → Segmentation). The min–max range next to the field comes from the same settings and prevents chunks that are too short or too long.
features.segmentationCardDesc: The default view shows each chunk as a card. An amber border flags anomalies (chunk outside the min–max range). Expand a card to read its full text. The rotate icon glows amber when manual edits are pending — click it to recompute chunks while keeping your adjustments.
features.segmentationEditorDesc: The top-right toggle switches to the segment editor: whole document as a single scrolling column, chunk boundaries as numbered horizontal dividers. Between any two paragraphs you can click '+' to add a boundary, '×' on an existing boundary to remove it. Scissors on long paragraphs split them in half. All edits are lossless: switching back to card view preserves manual decisions.
features.chunkActionsTitle: Chunk boundaries are fixed in the workspace
features.chunkActionsDesc: Once the document is loaded, chunk boundaries are fixed for that run: there are no inline split or merge actions in the document workspace or the Insights drawer. To redefine segmentation, go back to the import preview or reimport the document.
features.tokenDesc: The Statistics tab in the Insight panel shows total tokens and estimated session cost in real time, computed against official provider pricing. Counts are separated per stage and per judge. For Ollama the cost is zero because inference is local.
features.exportDesc: When there are completed chunks, the Export button in the Document panel of the sidebar opens a dialog where you pick format (.txt, .md, .html, .docx, bilingual .md). The chunk separator (blank line, HR, or asterisks) is available only for text formats (.txt and .md). The bilingual .md export includes source, translation, audit rating, and flagged issues for every chunk.
features.watchdogDesc: A background watchdog monitors chunks that linger in the 'processing' state longer than expected. If a chunk appears stuck — for example an Ollama model working on a very long context — a warning appears in the Index tab with a Cancel button to abort just that chunk without stopping the whole pipeline.
features.sandboxDesc: Alongside the document workspace there's a lighter Sandbox mode for quick experiments on short snippets. It is accessible from the workspace home or the new-project menu. It has no index, no stats, no coherence audit: use it to compare models or iterate fast on a single pass. Serious work stays in the document workspace.
features.footnotesDesc: When you import a DOCX or Markdown document with footnotes, Glossa separates them entirely from the translation process. Both the note text and the inline position markers are removed from what the model receives — the model sees clean body text only. The original document, shown in the editor, retains markers and notes exactly as they appeared. The note content is saved with the project. After translation you will need to handle footnotes manually: decide which notes to carry over, adapt their text to the target language, and place them where they make sense in the translated text — which may differ from their position in the original.
features.footnotesTipTitle: Why notes are not translated automatically
features.footnotesTipDesc: In a translation, a footnote often cannot be placed at the same position as in the original, and its text may need to be rewritten rather than translated word for word. Keeping notes out of the pipeline prevents the model from making arbitrary decisions about their placement and wording. You stay in control.
features.annotationsDesc: The Notes tab in the Insights panel lets you attach structured notes to individual chunks. Each annotation has a type (Comment, Doubt, Problem, Approved), a body text, and an optional anchor phrase that links it to a specific passage in the translation. Right-click any text in the translation pane and choose «Add annotation» to create one with the selected phrase pre-filled as the anchor. Audit issues also have a direct button to convert them into an annotation with anchor and content already filled in. Annotations are saved per-pipeline in the database and survive project reload.
features.annotationsTipTitle: Inline footnotes in the rendered view
features.annotationsTipDesc: When an annotation has an anchor phrase, Glossa inserts a GFM footnote marker ([^a1], [^a2], …) right after that phrase in the rendered translation view. The footnote definition appears at the bottom of the chunk. The stored draft is never modified — footnotes exist only in the rendered preview and disappear if the annotation is deleted.

context.title: Context & caching
context.intro: Glossa uses two mechanisms to keep translations coherent across chunks and keep inference costs low: a reference document block that gives each chunk access to its neighbors' source text, and a layered prompt structure that lets providers cache as much as possible between calls.
context.blobDesc: When translating a chunk, Glossa automatically sends the source text of nearby chunks alongside it as a reference block. The model uses this to maintain consistent terminology, names, pronouns, and style across chunk boundaries — without needing to see the whole document at once. For short documents the reference block covers the entire source text; for longer ones it covers a sliding window of neighbors. The reference block is provided as context only: the model is instructed to translate solely the current chunk, not the reference content.
context.cachingDesc: Every prompt is structured in three layers so the provider can reuse as much previously computed context as possible:
context.layer1Desc: Persona, structural rules, and glossary — identical for every chunk in the run. Cached once at the start and reused for all subsequent calls.
context.layer2Desc: Reference document block — shared by all chunks in the same neighbor group. Cached per group, so all stages for those chunks hit the cache for this layer too.
context.layer3Desc: Stage-specific instructions — sent fresh each time but are the smallest part of the prompt, so the cost is minimal.
context.isolationDesc: Each stage receives exactly the information it needs — no more. This prevents unintended retranslation and keeps each stage focused on its specific task:
context.stageTranslationDesc: Receives the source text of the current chunk and the reference document block. Produces the first-pass translation.
context.stageRefineDesc: Receives the source text, the reference block, and the output of the translation stage. Can compare original and draft to improve fluency and fidelity.
context.stageFormatDesc: Receives only the translated text from the previous stage — not the source text, not the reference block. This prevents the model from retranslating instead of just cleaning up formatting.
context.stageCoherenceDesc: Compares translated chunks against each other — not against the source. Receives a reference block of already-translated neighbors to spot terminology drift and continuity breaks across the document.
context.tipDesc: After the first chunk in a group is processed, subsequent chunks in the same group cost less because the provider reuses the cached layers. On long documents with many chunks the savings are significant, especially in editorial mode where three stages run per chunk.
context.cacheRetentionDesc: OpenAI uses two different cache policies. Full models (gpt-5.4 and above) use extended retention: the prefix stays cached for up to 24 hours, so each subsequent chunk benefits from the previous run's warm cache. Mini and nano models use in-memory retention only: the prefix expires after 5–10 minutes of inactivity. This explains why Refine (typically on gpt-5.4-mini) can show 0% cache hit even when the prompt is identical: if more than ~10 minutes passed between chunks, the cache has already expired.

streaming.title: Real-time streaming
streaming.p1: With Ollama (local inference) tokens are streamed in real time: text appears as it is generated, giving immediate feedback. With remote providers (Gemini, OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek) the response arrives in full once complete — there is no token-by-token streaming. In both cases the pipeline updates the chunk status as soon as the stage finishes.
streaming.p2: For Ollama the Rust backend opens a Server-Sent Events channel and Tauri relays tokens to the frontend with minimal latency. For structured stages (judge, coherence) — regardless of provider — the JSON is parsed only after the full response is received, whether streamed or not.
streaming.p3: On transient errors the system retries with exponential backoff up to three attempts. Timeouts are not retried: if the model is still computing a long response, Glossa waits rather than queuing a new request.

audit.title: Audit and quality
audit.intro: Glossa has two audit layers. The AI Judge evaluates each chunk right after the translation stages. The coherence audit is an optional second pass that examines the entire document. The judge produces five issue categories:
audit.glossaryIssue: The translation deviates from the terms defined in the Term Registry assigned to the project.
audit.accuracyIssue: The source meaning is not faithfully rendered: omissions, additions, contradictions.
audit.fluencyIssue: The rendering is awkward or unnatural in the target language, even if technically correct.
audit.grammarIssue: Grammatical mistakes, incorrect agreements, syntactic problems in the output.
audit.consistencyIssue: The same term or structure is rendered inconsistently across chunks in the document.
audit.reeval: After manually fixing a candidate translation, click 'Re-evaluate' in the audit panel to rerun the judge on that chunk only. Lets you iterate to the desired quality without running the full pipeline.
audit.issuesNav: Issue cards open the affected chunk directly, and — when the judge returns textual cues — try to focus on the relevant sentence with a search heuristic.
audit.coherenceDesc: The coherence audit is a separate pass that analyses the whole document at once, not chunk by chunk. It uses the Coherence Prompt from the Quality Control tab and is launched manually after all chunks are complete. Results appear in the Coherence tab of the Insights panel and surface terminological or stylistic inconsistencies between chunks — for example the same term rendered differently in different places.

projects.title: Projects
projects.intro: Projects live inside a translation workspace. The workspace contains books, Phrase Memory, and memory presets shared by those books; pipeline configuration remains specific to the opened project/pipeline.
projects.createDesc: From the workspace dashboard you can create, open, or delete projects. A new project is created in the active workspace and uses the current language pair as its initial default.
projects.saveDesc: Click the save icon at any time to persist the current state. When you reopen a project, configuration, stages, assigned glossary, chunks, translations, and notes are restored as you left them.
projects.importExportDesc: Use the upload icon to import a file (.txt, .md, .docx, .pdf) as the document source. When there are completed chunks, the Export button (↗) in the header opens the export dialog with format and separator options. Deleting a project also removes its pipelines, translations, logs, and saved project links.
projects.autosaveDesc: Glossa autosaves the project in the background on every meaningful state change: new completed chunks, translation edits, configuration updates. Autosave only activates once the project has a name: for new drafts, run the first Save manually to give it a name and enable autosave.
projects.backupDesc: The workspace dashboard exposes backup and restore. Backup exports local state to a portable .glossa-backup file; restore replaces local data with the imported snapshot. General app settings stay in Settings, while workspace Phrase Memory settings live in the dashboard.

providers.title: LLM providers
providers.intro: Glossa supports five providers. Each stage and the judge can use an independent provider and model. API keys are configured in the Settings panel.
providers.geminiNote: Google models. High throughput, low cost, solid quality on European languages. Great for high-volume translation and fast refine.
providers.openaiNote: OpenAI models. Elegant and versatile, good handling of stylistic nuance. Suited as a literary refine pass or a strict judge.
providers.anthropicNote: Claude models. Excellent on nuanced, literary text and less-common languages; tend to preserve tone and register. Strong refine and judge.
providers.deepseekNote: Chinese AI lab. Very competitive pricing, good multilingual support. A solid alternative to Gemini for volume translation.
providers.ollamaNote: Local inference, no API key, no data leaves the machine. Quality depends on the installed model; recommended for sensitive documents or offline work.
providers.gatingDesc: Features that require a remote provider — prompt refinement, preflight checks, running the pipeline on a non-Ollama provider — are disabled until the corresponding API key is configured in Settings. Key status appears as a `provider · model` label next to controls and as an inline notice in the pipeline Settings tab. Ollama is always enabled.
providers.security: API keys are stored in the operating system keychain (GNOME Keyring on Linux, Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows) when available. If the keychain is not accessible, Glossa uses an encrypted local file protected by a machine-local key. Keys are never written to disk in plain text, and never sent anywhere except the corresponding provider endpoint.

ollama.title: Using Ollama
ollama.intro: Ollama runs open-source LLMs on your own machine. No API key, no data leaves the computer. Suited to confidential documents and fully offline work.
ollama.installDesc: Download from ollama.com or use the install script:
ollama.pullDesc: Pull the models you want to use. Example of a popular pick for translation:
ollama.serveDesc: Ollama must be running in the background. On systems that don't autostart it:
ollama.useDesc: Open Settings — the Ollama section shows connection status and installed models. Pick 'ollama' as the provider in any stage or judge and select a model from the stage's dropdown.
ollama.recommendedDesc: For general translation: llama3.2 (3B), qwen2.5 (7B), gemma3 (9B). For higher quality on capable machines: llama3.3:70b or qwen2.5:32b. Models under 3B parameters tend to produce lower-quality translations — keep them for quick experiments.
ollama.thinkDesc: Some Ollama models support an extended reasoning step before responding. In the Ollama section of Settings you can set the Think level: off, low, medium, or high. Higher levels can improve quality at the cost of time and tokens. Only enable it for models that explicitly support thinking — on standard models it has no effect.

glossary.title: Library: dictionaries and templates
glossary.intro: The Library is a global panel (library icon in the header) shared across all projects. It has two tabs: Dictionaries, where you manage reusable term→translation collections, and Prompt Templates, where you manage the global collection of prompt templates.
glossary.libraryDesc: In the Dictionaries tab you can create new dictionaries, rename them with double-click, duplicate (Fork), delete, import terms from CSV/TSV, and edit entries inline by expanding a dictionary. A dictionary can be assigned as the active glossary of the current project with the Assign button.
glossary.csvDesc: The Upload button next to each dictionary opens a wizard that previews the first rows and asks for a strategy: 'Add/update' merges without touching existing terms, 'Replace all' wipes and reimports. Recognised headers: term/source/from for the source term, translation/target/to for the translation (case-insensitive); the notes column is optional.
glossary.projectDesc: In the configuration panel, Term Registry tab, you can pick the dictionary assigned to the project and edit entries inline. Edits act on the shared dictionary: the same dictionary can be assigned to multiple projects and entries are shared. The Save button appears as soon as there are pending changes.
glossary.highlightDesc: The Highlighter toggle in the chunk navigation bar enables or disables all highlights at once. When active: source terms are underlined, correctly translated terms have a green background, missing terms have a red background, and search matches have a yellow background. Colors are customisable in Settings → Highlights. Hover over a term to see the expected translation and notes.
glossary.searchDesc: The Search tab in the Insights panel lets you search for a word or phrase across all chunks at once — in the source text, translation, and audit findings. Each result shows a badge indicating where the match was found (source / translation / audit) and a snippet with the matched text in bold. Clicking a result jumps the workspace to that chunk, where the search term also appears highlighted in yellow.
glossary.auditDesc: The AI Judge explicitly checks adherence to the assigned dictionary and flags every deviation as a 'glossary' category issue, with severity and suggested fix. Particularly useful for technical, legal, or academic texts where terminology must remain stable.
glossary.templatesDesc: In the Prompt Templates tab of the Library you manage the global collection of templates, scoped by context: Stage (for translation, refine, format prompts), Audit (for judge and coherence), Persona (for system prompt openers). Create a template by setting name, context, and text; use the wand in the creation form to refine the text with an LLM. Saved templates are recallable via the bookmark buttons next to each matching prompt.

troubleshooting.desc: When something doesn't work, check the structured logs first. They're plain text — feel free to copy/paste them into a bug report.
